bibl.title: From Primed Concepts to Action: A Meta-Analysis of the Behavioral Effects of Incidentally Presented Words

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: The results of this meta-analysis showed small but robust significant effects of word primes on behavior and indicated that these effects obey the principles of value and goal satiation.

span.label: behavioral (conceptual) priming
span.quote: A meta-analysis assessed the behavioral impact of and psychological processes associated with presenting words connected to an action or a goal representation.

span.label: meta-analysis
span.quote: Our meta-analysis synthesized 352 published and unpublished effect sizes, obtained from research conducted in the US and internationally.

span.label: Meta-analysis is correlational, so the moderator relations reported cannot support causal inference.
span.quote: First, meta-analysis is a correlational research method.

span.label: Only word primes directly related to the measured behaviour were included.
span.quote: First, the current study only examined word primes that were directly related to the behavioral outcome assessed in the study.

span.label: Results may not generalise to other prime types (pictures, body poses) or to primes whose link to the outcome is less direct.
span.quote: This decision may limit the generalizability of our results because other types of primes (e.g., pictures, physical body poses) and primes that have a less clear relation with the dependent measure may produce different effects.

span.label: The null moderation findings hold only within the range of parameter values actually observed in the sampled studies.
span.quote: First, the present results are necessarily bound by the range of values observed in the meta-analysis.

span.label: behavioral priming
span.quote: Findings revealed a small behavioral priming effect ( d FE = 0.332, d RE = 0.352), which was robust across methodological procedures and only minimally biased by the publication of positive (vs. negative) results

span.label: meta-analysis
span.quote: A meta-analysis assessed the behavioral impact of and psychological processes associated with presenting words connected to an action or a goal representation. The average and distribution of 352 effect sizes (analyzed using fixed-effects and random-effects models) was obtained from 133 studies (84 reports) in which word primes were incidentally presented to participants, with a non-opposite control group, prior to measuring a behavioral dependent variable

span.label: perception-behavior
span.quote: the ideomotor principle into the postulation of priming effects based on the perception-behavior link. Bargh and his colleagues ( Bargh 1990 ; Bargh & Gollwitzer, 1994 ; Bargh et al., 1996 ) argued that stimuli available in the environment could be relevant to and therefore activate chronic behavior concepts and ultimately behavioral outcomes linked to those concepts. Associations between an environmental stimulus and these mental representations supposedly strengthen over time and increase the effects of merely perceiving these stimuli on subsequent actions

span.label: goal activation
span.quote: there was some evidence of persistence of goal effects over time. These results support the notion that goal activation contributes over and above perception-behavior in explaining priming effects. In sum, theorizing about the role of value and satisfaction in goal activation pointed to stronger effects

span.label: expectancy
span.quote: There was no evidence that expectancy (ease of achieving the goal) moderated priming effects. The worst is yet to come for priming

span.label: priming effects
span.quote: There was no evidence that expectancy (ease of achieving the goal) moderated priming effects. The worst is yet to come for priming

span.label: publication bias
span.quote: We addressed publication bias in four ways. First, we computed the fail-safe number on individual effect sizes ( N FS ), which corresponds to the number of unpublished negative findings (i.e., disconfirming findings that are either opposite to predictions or null) required to reduce a statistically significant result to nonsignificance ( DeCoster, 2009 ; Rosenthal, 1979 ; Rosenthal & Rosnow, 2008 ) using Rosenberg’s (2005) calculator. If the fail-safe number exceeds a cutoff value (5 k +10) specified elsewhere in the literature, publication bias is not deemed to be the driver of the synthesized effect

span.label: behavioral priming, OPERATIONALLY - and the inclusion criteria are the definition: word primes, INCIDENTALLY presented, a NON-OPPOSITE control group, and a BEHAVIOURAL dependent variable. Each clause excludes something. `Incidentally` rules out instruction; `behavioral dependent variable` rules out the judgement studies that most of this corpus's priming records use; and `non-opposite control` quietly excludes designs whose control condition primes the contrary concept, which would double the apparent effect
span.quote: in which word primes were incidentally presented to participants, with a non-opposite control group, prior to measuring a behavioral dependent variable. Findings revealed a small behavioral priming effect ( d FE = 0.332, d RE = 0.352), which was robust across methodological procedures

span.label: the effect, as a NUMBER rather than as an existence claim: d(FE) = 0.332, d(RE) = 0.352 across 352 effect sizes from 133 studies. `Small` is the paper's own word for it. The corpus holds dozens of records asserting that priming happens; this is the one that says HOW MUCH, and the size is what most of the surrounding controversy is actually about
span.quote: Findings revealed a small behavioral priming effect ( d FE = 0.332, d RE = 0.352), which was robust across methodological procedures and only minimally biased by the publication of positive (vs. negative) results

span.label: goal activation versus perception-behavior, ADJUDICATED WITHOUT A WINNER BEING DECLARED. The finding is an INCREMENT - goal activation `contributes over and above` perception-behavior - not a replacement. Two mechanisms this corpus has been collecting from separate papers, measured against each other for the first time, and the answer is both
span.quote: there was some evidence of persistence of goal effects over time. These results support the notion that goal activation contributes over and above perception-behavior in explaining priming effects. In sum, theorizing about the role of value and satisfaction in goal activation pointed to stronger effects

span.label: A MODERATOR NULL REPORTED IN THE ABSTRACT - expectancy, the perceived probability of achieving the goal, did not moderate priming. It was predicted to matter by two literatures that disagree about the DIRECTION (Forster: high expectancy strengthens pursuit; Locke & Latham: difficult goals intensify effort), so a null defeats both. A meta-analysis that puts its non-finding in the abstract alongside its finding
span.quote: There was no evidence that expectancy (ease of achieving the goal) moderated priming effects. The worst is yet to come for priming

span.label: the ideomotor inheritance, with the awkward part named: the perception-behavior account follows James's ideomotor model `ALBEIT WITHOUT THE CONSCIOUS (IDEO) COMPONENT FROM JAMES`. A mechanism borrowed from a nineteenth-century theory of voluntary action, with the consciousness that gave it its name removed - stated in the review's own parenthesis rather than dug out by a critic
span.quote: Evidence supporting the perception-behavior link followed the ideomotor model defined by James (1890; also see Carpenter, 1852 ), albeit without the conscious (ideo) component from James

span.label: extends → prior priming meta-analyses (Cameron, Brown-Iannuzzi, & Payne, 2012; DeCoster & Claypool, 2004; Van den Bussche, Van den Noortgate, & Reynvoet, 2009)
span.quote: Our meta-analysis is distinct from several other meta-analyses of priming in the field of psychology ( Cameron, Brown-Iannuzzi, & Payne, 2012 ; DeCoster & Clapyool, 2004 ; Van den Bussche, Van den Noortgate, & Reynvoet, 2009 ).

span.label: contradicts → Forster et al. (2007) and Locke and Latham (1990)
span.quote: Contrary to theorizing from both Forster et al. (2007) and Locke and Latham (1990) , there were no differences in the strength of priming across high- ( d FE = 0.252; d RE = 0.232) and low-expectancy ( d FE = 0.164; d RE = 0.166) levels (see B in Table 3 ).

span.label: extends → DeCoster & Claypool (2004)
span.quote: This effect is important and was not obtained in a prior meta-analysis of evaluative priming effects ( DeCoster & Claypool, 2004 ).

span.label: contradicts → Doyen et al. (2012)
span.quote: Thus, both of these replication attempts had a higher probability of failure than success, and the failures are not indicative of an earlier Type I error.

span.label: goal activation —contrasted-with→ perception-behavior
span.note: differs in: WHAT THE PRIME INSTALLS - a goal that pursues an outcome, against a direct perception-to-action potentiation. The meta-analysis finds the goal account adds explanatory work OVER AND ABOVE the perceptual one rather than replacing it, which is why this is contrasted-with and not distinct-from · strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE ADJUDICATION. Two mechanisms the corpus has been collecting from separate papers - Bargh2001 for goals, the ideomotor tradition for perception-behavior - weighed against each other over 352 effect sizes. The answer is an increment, not a winner, and the weight says so.
span.quote: there was some evidence of persistence of goal effects over time. These results support the notion that goal activation contributes over and above perception-behavior in explaining priming effects. In sum, theorizing about the role of value and satisfaction in goal activation pointed to stronger effects

span.label: expectancy —causes→ priming effects
span.note: direction on the measure: no-change · strength of the relation: 0.9 — A NULL RECORDED AS A DIRECTION, which is what `no-change` exists for. Two opposed literatures each predicted expectancy would matter - Forster (high expectancy strengthens pursuit) and Locke & Latham (difficult goals intensify effort) - and neither is supported. It is in the abstract, where a null is easiest to leave out.
span.quote: There was no evidence that expectancy (ease of achieving the goal) moderated priming effects. The worst is yet to come for priming

span.label: behavioral priming —same-as→ priming effects
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — The two names are used for one thing inside a single argument - `if BEHAVIORAL PRIMING requires goal-mediated processes, no PRIMING EFFECTS should emerge`. Weighted 0.85 rather than higher because the paper never states the identity; it displays it. Recording it is what lets a reader see why the paper's findings and its theory are phrased differently.
span.quote: Second, if behavioral priming requires goal-mediated processes, no priming effects should emerge when conditions are not conducive to goal activation. For example, conditions associated with lower value or expectancy with respect to a behavior or state may show no behavioral priming, particularly when there is insufficient time for motivational tension to escalate ( Chartrand et al., 2008) . Third, if both processes occur, then behavioral priming effects should be stronger in conditions leading to goal mediation
